purpose: Precisely calibrate 20 existing true AQA AS Physics first-school-mock short-recall card answer checkers without adding duplicate or long-answer cards.
scope: Particle classifications and interactions; pion, beta-plus, emission/absorption and fluorescent-tube energy levels; mechanics work, efficiency, centre of mass; parallel p.d.; RP2 fringe measurement, RP3 light gates, micrometer wire diameter, general practical uncertainties/gradients.
safeguards: Exact ID, original Physics subject, AS stage, mock flag, front and back, active status guards.
Original 3,345 core progress IDs, original prompts and answers are unchanged.
Actual production marker accepts each model answer and new correct response and rejects the wrong misconceptions.
No changes to full exam-question banks, maths first-mock scope, cloud sync or XP.
No claim of fully checked practical working or whole AQA specification completion.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Define a lepton.
rows.originalBack: A fundamental particle that does not experience the strong interaction.
accept: An elementary particle that does not feel the strong nuclear force.
reject: A hadron made from three quarks that experiences the strong nuclear force.
A lepton must undergo strong nuclear interactions to be a lepton.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is the pion's role between nucleons?
rows.originalBack: It acts as the exchange particle for the residual strong nuclear force.
accept: Pions can mediate the residual strong force between protons and neutrons.
reject: Pions are the exchange particles of the electromagnetic force between electrons.
Pions are exchanged to mediate gravity between nucleons.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Which lepton accompanies the positron in beta-plus decay?
rows.originalBack: An electron neutrino, νₑ (not an antineutrino).
accept: An electron neutrino accompanies the emitted positron in beta plus decay.
reject: An electron antineutrino is produced with the positron in beta plus decay.
A muon antineutrino replaces the electron neutrino in beta plus decay.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Why does each element have a characteristic line spectrum?
rows.originalBack: Its unique set of electron energy levels gives characteristic photon wavelengths.
accept: Each atom has distinct electron energy level gaps and therefore characteristic emitted wavelengths.
reject: All elements have identical atomic energy gaps and identical emission lines.
Each element emits a continuous range of all wavelengths without any discrete lines.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: How do fast electrons excite mercury atoms in a fluorescent tube?
rows.originalBack: They collide with atoms, transferring energy to electrons bound within the atoms.
accept: Collisions transfer kinetic energy from fast electrons to mercury atoms, exciting bound electrons.
reject: Electrons excite mercury without any collisions or transferred energy.
Fast electrons absorb mercury's ultraviolet light but never transfer energy to an atom.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is the centre of mass?
rows.originalBack: Point at which an object's mass may be treated as concentrated.
accept: The effective position where an object's total mass can be considered concentrated.
reject: The geometric centre regardless of how the mass is distributed.
The point where all external forces always cancel automatically.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is efficiency?
rows.originalBack: Useful energy output divided by total energy input.
accept: Useful energy transferred divided by total energy input, often expressed as a percentage.
reject: Input energy divided by useful output energy.
Useful energy output divided by energy wasted, ignoring total input.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is the work done by a perpendicular force?
rows.originalBack: Zero.
accept: Zero work, as the force component parallel to the displacement is zero.
reject: Maximum possible work because the force acts at ninety degrees to motion.
Work is force multiplied by displacement even for a force at right angles.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: In a parallel circuit, which quantity is the same across branches?
rows.originalBack: Potential difference.
accept: All parallel branches have the same voltage across them.
reject: Current must be equal in every parallel branch regardless of resistance.
The voltage drops across parallel branches must be added together.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Why use a micrometer for a wire's diameter?
rows.originalBack: Small diameter needs a high-resolution measurement.
accept: Its fine resolution allows accurate measurement of a very small wire diameter.
reject: A micrometer measures the resistance of the wire directly.
A micrometer is chosen because it cannot measure small distances accurately.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Which distance must be measured accurately in a double-slit practical?
rows.originalBack: Slit separation and slit-to-screen distance.
accept: Measure both the gap between slits and the distance from slits to the screen.
reject: Only the brightness of the laser beam needs measuring.
Only the width of the paper screen is required.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Why measure across several interference fringes?
rows.originalBack: It reduces the percentage uncertainty of fringe spacing.
accept: Measure across many fringe gaps so the total distance is larger and the relative uncertainty smaller.
reject: More fringes always mean a larger percentage uncertainty in each spacing.
Measuring several fringes removes all measurement uncertainties and guarantees exact values.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Why is a light gate useful for measuring acceleration?
rows.originalBack: It avoids human reaction-time error in timing.
accept: Electronic timing avoids human stopwatch reaction-time errors.
reject: Light gates increase errors caused by human reaction time.
A light gate removes all uncertainty in the length and timing measurements.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What makes a variable 'controlled' in an investigation?
rows.originalBack: It is kept constant to isolate the tested relationship.
accept: Keep it constant so only the chosen independent variable is being tested.
reject: Change the control variable at the same time as the independent variable.
Use the controlled variable as the response that is measured instead.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Why take repeated readings?
rows.originalBack: To identify anomalies and reduce random uncertainty.
accept: Repeats help identify outliers and reduce random uncertainty by averaging readings.
reject: Repeats remove all systematic errors such as a zero offset automatically.
One reading is always better because repeat measurements increase random error.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What does the y-intercept of a graph reveal?
rows.originalBack: The dependent variable when the plotted x-value is zero.
accept: The y value of the graph when the horizontal x value is zero.
reject: The horizontal x value at which y becomes zero.
The steepness or gradient of the graph at its origin.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is a fair comparison of two measured gradients?
rows.originalBack: Check whether their uncertainty ranges overlap.
accept: Determine whether the measured gradient intervals overlap within their uncertainties.
reject: Judge whether the graph lines have the same number of data points only.
Any two gradients must be equal if their graph lines cross.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Why do atoms produce emission line spectra?
rows.originalBack: Electrons occupy discrete energy levels, so only specific photon energies are emitted.
accept: Atoms have discrete electron levels, so only particular photon energies can be emitted in transitions.
reject: Atoms have a continuum of allowed electron energies and emit every possible wavelength.
All line spectra arise solely from splitting white light into colours.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Why do dark lines appear in an atomic absorption spectrum?
rows.originalBack: Atoms absorb photons whose energies match allowed upward transitions.
accept: Atoms take in selected photon energies matching allowed upward electron transitions, leaving dark lines.
reject: Atoms absorb every wavelength equally, so no individual dark lines can appear.
Dark absorption lines are caused by the atoms emitting additional photons at those wavelengths.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: How does a fluorescent-tube coating produce visible light?
rows.originalBack: It absorbs UV photons from excited mercury vapour and emits visible photons.
accept: The phosphor coating absorbs ultraviolet photons and emits visible light.
reject: The coating turns low-energy visible light into higher-energy ultraviolet without energy input.
The coating re-emits only X-rays rather than visible photons.
